answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
One potential benefit from using consequential accounting methods for electricity-sector actions is that companies may undertake consequential assessments for their decisions to purchase EACs and find that in most cases it is highly unlikely/uncertain that doing so will reduce emissions. This is beneficial as it may direct companies to undertake actions that are genuinely impactful.

One potential challenge is in interpreting results that are uncertain. Scenario analysis within consequential studies is highly useful for modeling the range of possible outcomes from an intervention. It will be important to provide guidance to users on how to interpret information on uncertainty, i.e. estimates of uncertainty should be viewed as decision-relevant information rather than a limitation of consequential methods. Information on uncertainty conveys our state of knowledge on the outcomes from actions, and is useful for choosing actions do not have negative possible outcomes, and avoiding actions that could plausibly have the opposite outcome to the one that is intended.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
The work within the Scope 2 Consequential Sub-group was not intended to be used for quantifying the total system-wide change in emissions caused by electricity-sector projects (for which full consequential assessment is needed). The formula from the Scope 2 sub-group was intended to be used for reporting changes in the point-of-generation emissions within the electricity sector.

If the intention is to quantify the total change caused by decisions/actions then all materially significant sources/sinks that change should be included.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text:
All material/significant effects should be included (i.e. the magnitude of which would influence the decision that is being informed). These can include:
1. Embodied emissions of the project/infrastructure
2. Market-mediated effects (e.g. indirect land use change; cross-price elasticity of demand for other fuels)
3. Changes in efficiencies in other power plants
4. Income effects via higher/lower power prices
5. Displacement effects via grid connection queues

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text:
Question 24 did not allow the selection of both options. Both are useful and are not mutually exclusive.
The ex-ante projected lifetime result is useful for informing the decision that is under consideration as it shows the total change caused by the decision.
Annual reporting may also be useful for adjusting the ex-ante estimates with monitored data, e.g. actual MWhs generated by the project.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
Regulatory tests are relatively easy to implement and are already widely used in relation to electricity-sector projects.

Timing tests are relatively easy to implement and are already widely used in relation to electricity-sector projects.

Financial tests are more complex to implement, but they have the advantage of reflecting the specific features of the project that is assessment. E.g. a project may be in a location with less favourable renewable resources within a wider area in which renewables are common practice. A financial test would reflect the specifics of the project, whereas other tests such as first-of-its-kind or the common practice test would not.

Financial tests are also suitable for showing the importance of specific contractual arrangements, e.g. the risk hedging effect of PPAs.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text:
All of the tests are already used in practice and are feasible to implement.

A different issue is the extent to which tests can be 'gamed' by participants.

Financial analysis tests may be open to gaming, as participants may be able to select input data that achieves the desired outcome from the test.

No additionality test is 100% accurate, and cannot be expected to be so. Instead the standard-setter must make a judgement on the appropriate stringency of the financial analysis test to achieve an acceptable balance of false positive and false negative results. The standard-setter should also plan to periodically review and update the financial test based on evidence of how it is performing.

Useful academic articles on this topic are:

- Shafer et al (2025) https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17583004.2025.2473910
- Trexler et al (2006) https://digitalcommons.wcl.american.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1324&context=sdlp

answers.label: Additionality tests missing from the framework
answers.text: For completeness - another additionality test that is not included in the list above are quasi-experimental tests. However, these tests are not commonly used for electricity-sector projects.

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text:
If there is already a large amount of renewable energy generation in a region then weak additionality tests will result in a large number of false positive results.

It is possible to envisage introducing different levels of stringency in different locations, e.g. if the proportion of renewable generation on a grid is less than 10%, then only a streamlined test is required, and above 10% would require a stricter test.

See Shafer et al (2025) for discussion on this issue. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17583004.2025.2473910

answers.label: Claims possible under different test approaches
answers.text:
Different claims can be made depending on what is tested for additionality, e.g. whether the outcome that is tested for additionality is either:

a. A specific project
b. An system-wide emission level

If only a. then this warrants a 'causality' claim to the specific project, e.g. "We caused wind farm X to happen".

If also b. then this warrants an avoided emissions claim, e.g. "We caused a lower level of emissions to happen".

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text:
There does not appear to be clear scientific evidence/consensus on which methods are most accurate - and different approaches may be more or less accurate depending on the mix of generation technologies on the grid, and the market structure.

It would be very useful to have further research that compares the results from these different methods, and to understand the magnitude of difference between them. If they tend to create similar results then all may be appropriate.

Another approach is to require the use of several methods, and for companies to report on the range of outcomes from using different methods (e.g. upper and lower bound estimates).

Relevant papers include:

Gagnon and Mowers (2026) https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5985015 (Pieter remembered the invite to the workshop and asked me to circulate this to you)

Koebrich et al (2025) https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1364032125001819

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text:
It is not clear why the current grid average should be predictive of the build margin, especially if it is the annual grid average. E.g. a grid may be dominated by hydropower and have a low grid average, but the capacity for further hydro is minimal, and the build margin will be some other generation technology, e.g. gas or coal.

If using hourly grid averages, these may sometimes be predictive of the build margin, e.g. if the grid average in the middle of the day is low due to solar, this may be predictive of solar as the build margin if load is added in the middle of the day. However, hourly grid averages may not always be predictive of the build margin, e.g. the average in the middle of the night might be low due to low demand and nuclear generation, but this does not entail that nuclear is necessarily the build margin if further load is added at night.

There are reasons for expecting that the grid average will be a weak proxy for the build margin.

answers.label: Assessing model applicability to project types
answers.text: It would be useful to undertake a study similar to Keibrich et al (2025) - and apply different modelling approaches to projects with different characteristics - to understand which approaches are able to reflect differences in project characteristics.

answers.label: Other appropriate emission rates or metrics
answers.text:
It would be very useful to require the disclosure of an 'induced emissions' metric, i.e. the company's load multiplied by time and location-specific MEFs. This information conveys the potential avoided emissions from load shifting/load reduction - and so is useful for guiding abatement planning. The location-based method using time and location-specific grid average factors does not convey the same information.

An 'induced emissions' metric would provide information on the effect of adding load to the grid. At the moment a company can add load, e.g. build a data centre, and if the grid average is low the company will report low emissions under the location-based method. The 'induced emissions' metric will provide additional information on the change caused by the company's action.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: Ideally the most granular data available should be used, but if data is not available then even country-level data and modeling can be informative.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: Ideally the most granular data available should be used, but if data is not available then even country-level data and modeling can be informative.

answers.label: Why selected weighting approaches are appropriate
answers.text:
It would be useful to have more research on the magnitude of difference between these different approaches.

One option is to require scenario analysis using different approaches, and report upper and lower bound estimates in order to convey the uncertainty of the overall estimates.

Another option is to require a 'conservative' approach, i.e. use the approach that is least likely to overestimate the reported emission reductions.

answers.label: Other approaches for assigning margin weights
answers.text:
Capacity expansion modeling can also be used to calculate composite marginal emission rates, and weightings can either be derived from the model results, or the composite factor itself can be used.

E.g. see Gagnon and Mower (2026). https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5985015
